utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Ladies and gentlemen, I am able to follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honour, I'm Patricia Sellers representing the Prosecution today. With me is co-counsel, Gramsci Di Fazio, and co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson; also our case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink, is with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you madam and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours and the colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence team for Mr. Naser Oric. We also have a legal assistant, Miss Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. And good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We just have one brief preliminary and Your Honour, it's more in the nature of an update, in terms of the projected time period, the Prosecution case. As I've discussed informally with the Defence this week, that we are still in the process of adding a few witnesses and removing witnesses. We've been informed by your legal assistant that we would follow that up with the proper motion asking your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is anything that needs to be formalised, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And we intend to be able to be in a position to follow that motion at least by mid next week, if not towards the end of next week, but to let you know we have formally been speaking to the Defence and are trying to update them so that in future -- their future preparation they would have knowledge of -- at least at this period of time people we have decided not to call and our anticipation of those called. I just wanted to state today that in our provisionary -- looking at our schedule it seemed as if we would be finishing somewhere between the 7th and 10 of June, and if that changes we will certainly get back to you. As I said this is provisional and I think by mid next week or the end of next week when we filed our motion we might have a slightly different date for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to make an effort to finish by the end of May, Ms. Sellers, a great effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours; we will convey that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary, try to make it a humungous effort, finish by the 8th of May. There are more reasons than one for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Finish by the 8th of May, Your Honour?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: End of May. End of May. Sorry -- my apologies if I said the 8th of May. Yes. 8th of May is an important feast day in Malta, so sometimes it does occur to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you live with that, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to get the names of the witnesses as soon as possible, at least the names so that our team can start working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that that I'm referring to. What I'm referring to is whether it is okay with you if we delay this filing till mid next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the essence of what I was going to say. Obviously we are uncomfortable with that because we were expecting the Prosecution to do that by the end of this week. However, if it's not possible, we would appeal to the Prosecution to do it as soon as possible. We got the name Okanovic on the list but we have no idea what the witness is supposed to testify about, and his testimony is coming up very soon and we would really like to get that information as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think you need to look into this. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That can be solved in an -- in an instant. He's the fellow -- who my colleagues will correct me if I'm wrong, I'm standing here, but he's the fellow who took the video of the planes over Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's it, so you will recall that video where you see the planes dropping bombs or whatever. And that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Please try to do your best to have this motion in place with all of the details by not later than Wednesday of next week. That's number 1. Number 2 is, try to work out your schedule in a way as to ensure that we try and finish by the end of May. When I say we try and finish, you finish your case by the end of May. And for the time being, I don't think I should add anything, because would we will obviously need to discuss the situation, the three judges and it's not something that I can decide on my own, for sure, how to go about it. But please do keep in mind that following the closure of the case by you, there is that important event that we had talked about that we need to put in place, number 1. There is the Rule 98 bis procedure that has to be followed, although this will be taking into account the amendments that have taken place and the time limit will be reduced considerably. And the important thing is that the Defence is put on notice well before they are expected, well before they are expected to start. And I have got nothing else to say. Let's bring the witness in. Madam Vidovic, are you going to finish with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday I made good progress and I'm going to try and do all I can. If the witness continues to reply in the same way, it is possible that I might finish. But in this part of my cross-examination, there will be documents, et cetera, so it might take a little bit longer. But I will do my best. After the second break, I will be able to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was not meant as pressure in any way, as you would have certainly gathered. The reason why I'm asking you is because we have the next witness - I'm not going to mention the name, her name - was supposed to start on Tuesday. Because I asked Madam Vidovic the question because, I have enough experience to know where she stands with this witness already. And I do anticipate that if she doesn't finish today, she will finish pretty early on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I would have thought so as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in that case I would suggest that whoever is proofing the next witness, witness number 40, I wouldn't know who it is. I don't want to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The witness is flying in on Saturday and is going to be started to be proofed on the Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try -- the whole idea is, please do understand me. I mean, it's -- last thing I want to do is to waste time. It's not that I, my two colleagues, yourselves have got nothing else to do. I mean we all have a lot of work to do. But the thing is, I have a responsibility. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I gather that what you would like is for the witness to start after the completion of this particular witness on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Start on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean immediately after. I didn't say immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is an extra hour, that's no big deal, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I gather what Your Honour is driving at. Yes, we will comply with that. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. And also because the more time we save, the earlier we can finish and the easier it will be for you to regulate --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Counsel who is handling that witness will be informed and they will be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There is just one very small matter. Should Madam Vidovic finish with this witness at the -- today and should something unusual happen, say, she finishes 20 minutes or 15 minutes beforehand, could I put off my re-examination until Monday? Because I haven't had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to be able to read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I asked Madam Vidovic in my heart of hearts I knew that -- what the answer was going to be. It's possible that she finishes today, but more likely that she overflows on to Monday, but that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All I'm saying is I would like to be able to read the transcript and prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. I don't think there will be any problems there, but don't use this as a stratagem to delay bringing the next witness until Tuesday. Understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's perfectly understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with your testimony. We'll do our best, very best to progress as much as possible today. I don't promise you that we will finish today. Probably we will overflow to Monday, which would give you an opportunity to spend a weekend here in this beautiful city hoping that the weather will be your friend. But much depends on how you answer the questions. In other words, how efficient you are in your answers. Yesterday, particularly, you were extremely efficient and the day before. You have been taking my advice, answering the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Please try to maintain that. I hope you had a good rest and that you have been able to contact your family. All right. Please, sit down and let's start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wanted to remind you, you are still testifying under oath. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we stopped when you were saying that you did not accept Naser as commander. You had your own unit at the very centre of Srebrenica, wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was known as Hakija's men?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 100 people in that unit in 1992, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 maximum. And sometimes less than that. Between 60 and 100 men. It varied.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Oric used to come to Domavija hotel and to ask you to help out in certain cases?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not write any reports to him?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You sent your men into action on those occasions when you were in agreement and if you were in agreement with the action; is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you were made chief of police at Srebrenica, following the demilitarisation in April 1993, you were never a member of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not on the list. I saw it afterwards, but well that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness the Prosecution document P80. P80, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, it's supposedly a document from the staff of Territorial Defence for Srebrenica dated the 19th of September, 1993. And the title is delivery of data with regard to the formation and structure of the armed forces at Srebrenica in the past period. It consists of six pages. First of all, there are references to the first, the 2nd and 3rd formation or structure. I would like to draw your attention to page number 4. Can you take a look. There is a big computer number there, 02075846. Could you please place the English version of this document on the ELMO, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking of page 3 in the English version. Correct? Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we are referring to page 6 of the English version, item 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote to you what it says on page 4, "Independent Srebrenica Battalion based in Srebrenica, commander Safet Mujic, 849 conscripts, comprising five companies." I would like to ask you to look at the last line of this document. It says "the Fifth Company based in Srebrenica, Commander Hakija Meholjic." In other words, according to this document, it would appear that your company was a part of the independent Srebrenica battalion under the command of Safet Mujic. Now, Mr. Mujic, Safet has never actually been your commander, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some attempts to that effect, but I don't know. I would say not. There were attempts at organising that, but I can't really claim that he was my commander, because he was never in a position to order me anything whatsoever. So, if I may just clarify. There had been attempts as I was saying, I mean my life is actually too short to cram into it all the experiences I've had. And I can't go into every single detail. But, yes, there had been attempts to that effect, but I don't think they were successful. Naser will know better and you, of course, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in practice, de facto he had never been your commander?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So it is true that this document contains wrong information?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A reference to Bektic Nedzad is a bit surprising as the person in charge of security. I mean, Naser will know, but I think he was appointed at a later stage. Don't misunderstand me. I think it happened at a later stage. Perhaps he was already there at the time, but I don't know. This is the first I've seen of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I'm going to put this question to you in a different way. This structure is on paper, in case this is an authentic document, but at any rate, the reference to you does not reflect the real state of affairs in as far as your unit was concerned?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your testimony, you have told us that Oric had appointed you as commander of a certain area in order to, in March 1993, defend a certain part of Srebrenica territory. You yourself volunteered the information whereby you said that Hadjin [phoen] had been prepared to do, he wouldn't have been in a position to order you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I did want it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of your testimony, I can conclude that you were very familiar with Zulfo Tursonovic and Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo and Akif were both people of a certain age with some life experience?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were slightly older, but as to their fitness mentally and physically, well I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about elderly people here. You told us that on one occasion Naser wanted to meet with you with regard to the Zaluzje action, but Zulfo opposed your presence and the meeting did not take place, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Zulfo's wish was -- actually took precedence over Naser's decision?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Zulfo Tursonovic, on one occasion, in the course of 1992, said: "If Hakija's men are going to fight in this battle, I won't be there." Zulfo Tursonovic's character was such that you could not really oppose him.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. And Mr. Oric knows and I do know that he found the situation difficult. And as to the characters of the people in charge of those local units, well they varied. We had certain people of character and, well educated people who had fled Srebrenica and those who remained, well, it was a bit difficult. We had to adjust to the circumstances at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree that Zulfo Tursunovic went along with Naser only on those occasions when he felt like it? When he felt it was convenient?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I can only assume that, but I was not with them when they were talking to one another, and I'm unable to comment on that. But I know Zulfo. I mean, he's a bit difficult, if he didn't want to do something there was nothing you could do about it. And how Naser managed, well I don't know. That's why I said that Naser probably found himself in a difficult situation. That's why I was against its appointment because I thought that he was just not up to the task of dealing with all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I mentioned a certain battle, and the participation on your and Zulfo's part in a certain battle. Quite simply, Zulfo was free to decide whether he wanted to join in or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking a question about Asliza [phoen], he went and he lost between three or five people at the very beginning and then he left straight away. He didn't do anything at all. So, yes, he could. He was not accountable to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same way you mentioned yesterday that Akif Ustic went into action on his own initiative and according to your opinion, without Naser's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. And I minded. I mean, I said, okay if Naser didn't know, fine. But Hamdija and myself, we didn't know either. And we were supposed to be his subordinates. So if he's battalion commander and he doesn't tell his company commanders what he was doing, well -- and then he ends up wounded or loses between eight or 12 people in a certain action, well this was a disaster.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about an action in which Akif Ustic was wounded. So that was the action that he undertook on his own initiative?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the month of June 1992, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really tell you. June or July. Don't press me on the dates, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was an action in the area south of Srebrenica, am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The upper area. When I say the upper area, it is to the south-east, perhaps. One should look at the map, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Isn't it true that your opinion is that Akif did things upon his own initiative, without informing Naser and at any rate without asking for any permission from Naser?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he did when he went to Zaluzje. And he took his men there and about 20 people were killed and he himself was killed. He was just doing everything on his own initiative and that's when he messed up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you agree with me, in relation to the nature of the relationship between these people, that is to say that Zulfo and Akif accepted Naser as commander, but they did not feel bound to inform him about their activities or to follow his orders, except in those situations where they felt like it. Can you agree? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I have decided to testify in public and I have to go back there and live there and I'm going to reiterate what I said before. I'm accepting all moral and criminal responsibility for everything I've said, so my opinion is this. I am convinced of that, but Naser was more in touch with them than I was, but since I know several things on the basis of my own personal experience, when Akif and myself were together when I was his boss, when I was elected to that position by the population in the beginning, so even then he did things on his own initiative and some of these things were disastrous. For example, when his cousin was killed, that was also something that he did single-handedly. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Thank you very much. Akmija -- Akmija's people or Akmija's [as interpreted] army was under the command of Ahmet Tihic at Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and his nickname was Tica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true that Ahmo Tihic was also, to a great extent autonomous independent, is it known to you as well?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he acted autonomously. He was a commander. I don't know what kind of a unit he had up there, either a battalion or a company, but he did act independently. I don't want to speak certain things about him. He's dead. He was more into some other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not about crimes, but in connection of seizing some grain and then selling it to Muslims, et cetera. You have to understand, it is not a simple task for me to be here. I've come here to tell the truth. Not against Naser. Not to speak in favour of him. But to tell the truth so that the people can continue with their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meholjic. It is known to you, is it not, that certain commanders led by Mr. Tihic and leaning towards the hard-liners of the SDA wanted to establish a completely separate army, is it known to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naser is guilty for that. He accepted Ibran and Ibran came to -- with a task to divide us even more than we were divided before. And they invited me to take part in this, but I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Ibran. What kind of Ibran was he?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Ibran Mustafic, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask the usher to show the witness a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not objecting. I'm merely making an observation. The witness has just given evidence about something involving Ibran. I don't know if Your Honours understood that, that portion of evidence, but I have some trouble understanding what was meant. It's a question of Ibran coming along and not -- and Naser accepting it. Accepting what? It's unclear. I don't know if you want to pursue it or not. It's not my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to pursue it to be honest with you to by asking the witness who sent this Ibran. Who sent this Ibran? Because otherwise it doesn't make sense. I agree with you. It does make sense, I mean, because you can come to conclusions, but who sent Ibran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ibran was the president of the executive council of Srebrenica before the war. Then he was in Sarajevo as a delegate at the republic level, as it was before the war. Towards the end of 1992, miraculously, Ibran managed to reach us from the direction of Rogatica, through Zepa, during war circumstances. And since he was a leader of the SDA, he started proselytising. We don't need this kind of army, et cetera and we -- our answer was: "How can you say that? You fled." But Mr. Tihic and I -- and he were in it together but I was against it. Not because of anything else, but because of the appointment of that man, if things were different I could have been in the dock instead of in the witness stand. But the situation was as it is and there was some internal fraction that started then. When I'm talking about Ibran. In 1995 when Srebrenica was about to fall, and Mr. Oric was there [as interpreted], at an Assembly, an Assembly of the municipality. Ibran Mustafic demanded publicly to establish radio contact with Momcilo Krajisnik to get us out of Srebrenica. After that Srebrenica fell. He was detained and exchanged. Many people were killed who were retarded, retarded, who didn't know who they were, what was -- but he managed to stay alive. If I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's keep to what is relevant. You also said that Oric, Naser Oric accepted him. What did you exactly mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he accepted him as a person, but I did not mean accepted him in this sense. I would have told him, "Go away," because what he left behind him is a disorganised group. He was president of the executive council. He left us at the mercy of the headless, without leadership, and it was my duty, as a policeman to defend the lives and property of citizens in extraordinary circumstances. This is what I was paid for.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Meholjic. So Oric accepted him as a person. Just a slight correction. I see that in 1995 Naser was -- you said that Naser was not in Srebrenica before the fall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what happened because I wasn't following the transcript and was doing other things at the same time. But I heard him say the opposite. And in fact, if you look at line 12, he said in 1995 when Srebrenica was about to fall and Mr. Oric was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't there. He wasn't there. Well, everybody knows that. It's generally known thing that Naser was outside of Srebrenica then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I will ask the usher to show you a document. It is a document by the police station of Srebrenica or public security station of Srebrenica. 4th of April, 1994. It is an assessment of the political and security situation in the demilitarised zone and in connection with what we spoke about. I would like to read out to you a passage from page 2 where it says: "At meetings held on Saturdays in the house of Hamid Efendic and on other days with Ahmo Tihic plans are made to belittle the fight of the self-organised people and they determine who will take which position when they come into power." You were aware of this situation, that they were trying to organise an army and you reported that fact. I see this is a report from 1995. But you had sent reports on this even before that date?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want this document to be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add, this document was forwarded to the 2nd Corps, because the Presidency accepted my report in its entirety and forwarded to 2nd Corps to inform them of the situation in the protected zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want this written material to be tendered into evidence and to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do so, Madam Vidovic, I see this document -- at least what we have been given -- the first two pages, 096 and 097, followed by the English equivalent, right, which consisting of three pages. Then there are a number of pages in handwriting, about five, six pages or something like that. Followed by three pages, three pages in English. I am prone to presume that this is the same document, one in typewritten form, one in handwritten form. The English translation, in each case, is not exactly identical. It seems that they have been translated by different persons at different times. But I want to establish that that is correct. If that is correct, then we need to move to the following questions. Number 1, I would like the witness to look at the typewritten document which has the last number 096 and 097 and on the second page, there is a stamp and a signature under, or upon -- over the name Hakija Meholjic. And I would like him to confirm that that is, indeed, his signature and that that stamp is an authentic stamp. That's number 1. And secondly, I would then refer the witness to the other document, which is handwritten, in handwritten form, which starts with 098 and finishes with 103, and ask him if he is in a position to inform us -- to tell us whose handwriting that is, if he can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you asked me, this is my signature on this and my stamp on this document. And this is true. And I fully endorse that. Regarding this handwritten document, I dictated and I believe that Resid Efendic wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add, this handwritten document is a more handwritten document is a -- more expansive in its context. I will repeatedly use that document and this is the reason, just to save us some time. I'm explaining this so that we can tender the whole document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to tender the two documents together? Or do you want to separate them?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would separate them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Thank you very much for your suggestion. I can separate these two documents. So I propose that the document from 24th of April, a two-page 3906 and 3906 and 9097 to be given an exhibit number, and the document with the numbers 9098 to 9103, to be given a different exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one. 096 and 097, this will be D.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit number D243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 243. So. Right. And the other one will be Defence Exhibit 244. Do you have a clip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you put the previous question and you referred the witness to the document, were you referring him to the first one of these two documents? Or to the second? Madam Vidovic? You told the witness, I'm reading from page 2 and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked the witness to take a look at the first document, but to save some time, the witness took a look at the second document and said that he knows of the document. He dictated it. I didn't want to ask him additional questions because he had already confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I will now go back to the topic of Ahmo Tihic. Ahmo Tihic, is it not, he had a great deal of influence in the area where he was active?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a pre-war activist of the SDA and he had some influence on decisions that affected the area of Srebrenica as well, am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, is it true, is it not, that Oric could not issue orders to Tihic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here now, you are bringing me into a very awkward position. I believe and I've told you, to the Chamber and everybody, that Naser knows that I did not attend meetings and I cannot comment whether he had any quarrels, whether he had made concessions, whether he could or could not, at those meetings where I wasn't present. It was very difficult to issue orders to Tihic. He was an SDA hard-liner. So it was very difficult. That's why I said that Mr. Oric was surrounded by some people who suggested some bad things to him. I believe that it was very difficult for him to get on top of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These groups of people, up until the establishment of the 28th division and later on, they were known as Zulfo's people, Nedzad's -- Zulfo's people, my people?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "my people," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, perhaps could you make clear, on the period of time we are talking about, was it the beginning of 1992? Or the end of 1992 or 1993, because I think there has been more than a year that the relationship may have been the same or it may have changed between the people who are in discussion here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about a period during 1992 until April 1993, are we not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Meholjic, although the headquarters and the staff was established and existed, objectively in the field in 1992 and the winter offensive in 1993, in essence we are talking about individual, independent village-based armed groups of people?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They covered that part of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were attempts to organise those, the structure of those groups?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Naser tried to subsume those groups under his command, am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, you are right. But what happened later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you agree with me if I said that throughout 1992 and early 1993, until March 1993, armed forces in Srebrenica did not resemble a proper army?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how it is, a proper army is something completely different. You have to understand the situation we were in. Secondly, those were not soldiers living in barracks. These were people who would go back home for the night. And so if we had a meeting arranging an attack, then we would ask commanders how many people can you get for the fight, as if we were going for a harvest. And then people would say: "Well tomorrow I can gather ten people," et cetera. But very soon -- very often we would get less people than was announced, because there was no structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I could understand, there were agreements made. There was no line of command?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no line of command for me. I cannot accept that there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These people in these armed groups, they did not wear uniforms or they had very little -- very few uniforms, army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people got, people from Nurif came and people were ill-dressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They had very few arms, no weapons were arranged for them. They had to take it from the enemy, is it right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If my group which had 18 automatic rifles, 20-odd semi-automatic, and one machine-gun, then you can -- and -- we were the best-armed group, then you can imagine how it was for the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Food was not secured for the fighters?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except that I did for my men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no ranks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not allowing the short interval of time that I appealed for yesterday and the day before. And I can see that the interpreters are finding it difficult to catch up with both of you. And that will reflect in the transcript, because we are missing things then. So, please, this applies to both of you, including you Madam Vidovic, because you're doing exactly the same as the witness is. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about ranks. There were no ranks?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no breads, let alone ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no patches. There were no markings by which the troops could be distinguished from civilians?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the bands are concerned, the bands that the fighters used to wear in actions, for their families this was no secret. Anybody who followed them could use those bands, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fighters of the Srebrenica area were mostly persons who swapped their tools and took to arms, am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no circumstances or conditions in place that would enable the commander to exercise the effective control over the troops that were supposed to be subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no", does that mean that you confirm my statement?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Is there was nothing in place to provide for an efficient control. Not even the organised military of the United States cannot control all of its troops, let alone us. We were not organised. Secondly there were no corps. There was no mechanism to punish a soldier. You could only beat him or chase him out of your ranks. There were no institutions as such in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever there was on paper, in terms of the military organisation at the time during the war, year of 1992 and early 1993, did not reflect the reality of the matter.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please this evidence is going to be meaningless unless we know what piece of paper, unless the -- unless Madam Vidovic says or makes it clear that she is referring to every document that was shown to the witness in court, or, if not, what other paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you did see the paper that we showed you a little while ago that refers to the organisation of units on the ground and my last question was relative to that particular document. Please, whatever there was on that paper, in terms of the military organisation, during 1992 and early 1993, did not actually reflect the reality of the matter.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't like things half cooked. You are referring to P80? P80? Witness, could the witness be shown P80 again, please. To my knowledge you were only referred to one small part on P80 and that was on page 4 in your language, page 6 in our language. Not in our language, in English language, in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Your Honour but he also mentioned Nedzad Bektic as the commander of the security organ and he said that this did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Look at the document again, please and I want to make sure that before you give a final answer on Madam Vidovic's question, you have gone through the entire document. Did you see this document before coming here to The Hague? Were you ever shown this document before coming here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So please take your time and have a look at it. And then at the end, please tell us how much we, the three Judges, ought to rely on this document. Yes, you can put the English version on the ELMO, madam, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have had a look at the document and when I read the titles, it seems there were more battalions than the troops themselves. And if you wish to hear my comment, I will be very brief and I will provide you with a comment. Whether this is a credible document or not, I can't be a judge of that. But I can say that it -- if you look at this document, you get the impression that something existed, but there was nothing. Hakija, when I read here "poljek," [phoen] "battalions,", "millions of battalions," and they did not have even two hens let alone the troops that are mentioned here. I believe that this has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the situation on the ground. This looks like a very good homework that somebody was given to do and did really very well. However, this document has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, look at the last page of the document, where it is purported to be stamped and signed by Bektic Nedzad. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 6. Page 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here, the stamp first of all, I don't understand the stamp. It is very small. As for the signature, I never saw the signature before. I never saw Bektic's signature before, so I can't tell you anything about his signature. If it is his signature, then he's the one who confirm that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, one final question, just for the record also, because Madam Vidovic referred to this. It also says -- correct me if I am wrong -- "nacirnek," [phoen] Does that mean chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it says something else. [B/C/S/ spoken]. Does it say he is supposedly signing as chief of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he was chief and if he did sign that, I suppose that he took it upon himself the responsibility to act on anything that was done by the troops on the ground. This would have been his duty. However, I know that he arrived later. I don't know that he was there during this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, in or about the 19th of September 1993, are you telling us that Nedzad Bektic was not in Srebrenica? Or are you telling us that he may have been in Srebrenica but you cannot tell us if he was chief of intelligence and security at the time, 19 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19th September 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1993. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or 1993? Okay, 1993, he was there. He was assistant commander. That already existed. However, this does not have anything to do with the organisation on the ground. This is a census. This has to do with the creation of the 28th division. This is -- this does not reflect the period of war activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. He's back to you, Madam Vidovic. I tried to help you and also in response to the point made by -- very valid point made by Mr. Di Fazio. He's back to you. You are free to ask him any question you like on this document, any further question. However, let's try to avoid repetition and we are still -- we are still away from the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if I may provide you with an explanation? If this document was issued in September 1993, Hakija Meholjic was no longer in the army. He was the chief of the public security station, so how did my name find itself there?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this very valid and valuable explanation. I'm going to move on to another topic. The term battalion is mentioned here. You've also mentioned the term battalion on several occasions. If we're talking about a battalion within the Srebrenica TO in May 1992, you're not talking about a duly-established unit in a modern army such as the JNA was at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. We were -- we had to give it a name and we just used the terms from the JNA. We did not have any other terms at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, you were talking about a certain number of people who were fighting, a group of people who were fighting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the same refers to the terms that you used, such as company, brigade, and so on?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, these were not duly-established and equipped units with all of the things that these terms imply in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was shown some documents here and I saw that Zulfo said, "People were lying to each other; we don't have that many people." It was an arbitrary way of giving names to certain groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the character or nature of combat units in Srebrenica in 1992, you said, about you're unit, on page 17, as follows: "Our men did not have to be anywhere if they didn't want to be there. They could flee. They could run. They could go to Tuzla, or they could change their unit." Your unit, if I may call it so, was better organised than other units in Srebrenica because it did have some sort of barracks, which was the Domavija hotel.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, even in your units, your men could leave -- could go as they wished and come back as they wished. You couldn't force them to do anything?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't force them to do anything. They would go. They would come back. Some I chased out of my unit if they didn't behave the way I wanted them to behave.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify a matter in the transcript. So they could go -- they could join another unit if they so wished?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words people did not necessarily belong to the units in their villages. In your unit there were men from different locations. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know it is correct that you could not force able bodied-men to fight. They could leave without being held accountable for that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could do that and there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in Srebrenica, in the course of 1992 until the demilitarisation, people acted on a voluntary basis. Am I right in saying that, and this was the case even up to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about this issue, I would kindly ask you to assist us with the following thing. When you were talking about actions, you were mentioning different people, Zulfo's men, Akif's men, Naser's men, your own men, and we heard that Oric was the TO commander as of May 1992. However, when you were describing people who fought after the month of May, 1992, you wouldn't say that all of these men were Naser's men?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They couldn't be. How could they have been?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, is it not, that local commanders kept their command of their men?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Realistically speaking, Naser had real command power over his men? Did he or did he not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did. He had power over his men. He did not have power elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about all of these actions, what actually happened is that different commanders, with their respective troops, would go into action and that these actions were coordinated amongst themselves in order to be efficient?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would know who was on our left flank, who was on our right-hand flank, who was following us, because if you enter the 2nd, then the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't hear the end of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Vidovic because we have a problem. The interpreters did not hear the -- your answer completely. So if you could repeat it, please. You said: Yes, we would know how was on left flank, who was on our right flank, who was following us, because if you enter the 2nd, and then the interpreters got lost in a good sense. Could you finish your sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was given my territory, I would be independent in working out how I would enter. This was not worked out at the staff. Every commander would have to work out his part of task, the task that he had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom? A task would have been given by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At meetings where we sat down and we discussed the plan. This was not a proper plan. The plan was just to attack a certain area for a certain reason. Again, we were discussing the number of people that we could count on and then one commander would come from one direction. Another from another direction. It was the staff. It was not myself who could call such meetings. It was the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Meholjic, the staff was the place where you agreed on the forthcoming actions. Oric was not the person who issued orders on the actions. It was the commanders who agreed on those actions, amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. But let me clarify that. I don't know when there were those meetings of the staff and what decisions were made. I know that when I was invited to such meetings, Osman Osmanovic would chair, and he would inform us that an attack was to be carried out. It was not Naser who would issue orders to the effect, "Okay, we are going to do this." We would sit down. We would talk. Somebody would say "I don't have any ammunition, is there anybody who can provide me with some? Does anybody have any spare ammunition to give me?" And this is how things happened. I don't know whether I've made myself clear or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were talking about the actions in which you didn't participate, you said that you assumed that Naser or somebody that he authorised to do that, had been in command of those attacks. This was your assumption, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. Somebody has to issue an order, but I did not have in mind the proper military command, artillery, or this or that because we did not have that. But there would be people who would be designated for coordination, one or two persons. For example, if Naser said let's withdraw, it could have been him, or it could have been me. And whenever this was said we would withdraw. It could not have been said by somebody that -- whom the fighters didn't know. I don't know whether I'm making myself clear at all. There was a person, there had to be a person who had to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you assumed that it would have been much more effective to have one commander, but you don't know whether this really happened in those actions, although it was a good idea. It would have been a good idea?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could have pulled out from any action and nobody could do anything to you. However, if you wanted to save your face and if you took the task upon itself, then you would proceed and there were no disputes about that. So we never disputed about that part of the action. Once you took upon the responsibility, you carried through.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of my question with regard to the actions was as follows: You assumed that it would have been much more effective to have one commander in the actions in which you didn't participate. However, you don't know whether this is what happened in practice?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened on the ground. When my men were sent to the ground, they didn't have any -- they didn't make any problems and Mr. Oric knows that whenever I took responsibility upon myself, I followed through. And whatever I did, I am ready to take responsibility for my actions, because I was the one who was in charge, who was responsible. And it is true that it would have been very good that the command could have been exercised from one place, that is the state of lack of organisation and the lack of structure. And in our circumstances, things could not have been done better than they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you testified yesterday about the incident during which you were surrounded at the Domavija hotel because Naser thought that you were in charge of some actions and that you had not informed him, I would like to come back to that and ask you a few questions about that. First of all, do you agree that he was under the influence of the fact that some people had died, that this could have been the fact that people had died because the action was not coordinated and that he was actually concerned about the futile loss of life. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also agree that on one occasion you were not satisfied when Hustic did not inform you about an action that he took?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that all those who fought in Srebrenica wanted to know what was going on and that they were dissatisfied if they were not informed about the actions, because this could have had repercussions on them, their men and their respective territories. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. If those territories were close to each other. And the story was entirely different if those territories were far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what I meant. It could have been dangerous for everybody in Srebrenica if actions were not coordinated and if they were not under some sort of control?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo, Akif, Hamdija, they also wanted to be informed about the actions that were undertaken by others?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. They were members of that staff. For what it's worth the staff was there to coordinate things to the extent that it was possible. People had to talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is a good moment for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Vidovic. We will have a break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, you testified yesterday about meetings at which military matters were discussed. First of all, do you agree that quite a few meetings took place where you were not present and such matters were discussed on those occasions, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to meetings that you attended, when Prosecution asked about whether Naser was in a position to influence the decision making process, you answered: "By all means everybody could, especially him. I think he was the commander. It is assumed then that he should have more influence than others." First of all, can you agree that there is a difference between what is assumed to be the case and what is indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact in the period of time between September 1992, until demilitarisation, judging by the war diary, you, at staff meetings or joint staff meetings between -- with the Presidency as well, well you were present there twice in September and October 1992, is that correct? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I did not look through all the papers, but I did attend some meetings. I can't really I say. Probably it transpires from the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you attended those meetings rarely?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask the usher to show the witness P 84, it's an exhibit which has to do with the minutes of the meeting on the 3rd of October, 1992. The page number is -- no, sorry. The end is PO46. But at the same time, I would like you to show the witness the pages P047 and 5048. So it was not "P", but it was 5046, 5047, and presumably 5048. So, in the English version, basically, those are the pages from 4 through to 6. Mr. Meholjic, I would like you to take a look at the first page, the number is 5046. It's the computer number. And you can see that Osman is reported to be speaking. And you can see as the Prosecution showed to you yesterday, that it was about preparing for action at Fakovici. Because in the fourth sentence of what he is satisfying, it says, there is a three-barreled gun at Fakovici and so on and so forth, and there are references to Fakovici. Do you agree that it is a meeting at which actions at Fakovici in September 1992 was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at the names of the people who took the floor in preparing for that action. On page 2, there is a reference to your name. You seem to be saying -- well, there is a reference to Hakija and yesterday you indicated it to refer to you. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to go back to page 1. You can see that the reference is to Osman. Then Akif, and then Osman again, and then Hamid. And on page 2, can you turn to page 2, please. Sakib, Ahmo, Zulfo, and then Osman once again. And on page 3, Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite follow you. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't follow you either.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't follow either, Madam Vidovic. So if you can be a little bit more helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were following me all right on the first page, which ends with number 5046.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do hope the Judges could follow me with regard to page one otherwise I will have to repeat what I said in relation to page 1. On page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 1 is 5046.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be simpler if Your Honours just say, "on page 5046."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be simpler. I think that is why the confusion arose, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this suggestion. On page 5047, Mr. Meholjic, there is reference to your name, Hakija and then -- did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you have "Sakib" just underneath, answer number 4.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then in number 6, you have Ahmo, and then number 7, Zulfo. 8, Osman. I would like you to turn the page and look at page 5048.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And there is a reference to the name Hamdija here, is that right? I don't see any other names here except for Hamdija. Take a good look.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Hamdija. But do I need to read anything out to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, you don't need to. I'm going to ask you a question and my question will be referring to all these names. You, in your testimony, stated that Naser attended that meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by these minutes, it would appear that he didn't say a single word. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony yesterday, I'm going to ask you something else altogether. So this question is not in relation to the question you've just answered. So in the course of your testimony yesterday, and in relation to this same meeting, you said that Naser said that you would get the time you needed in order to demine the area in the direction in which you were supposed to go. But simply what he said was not adhered to by others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser told me: "You will get that." And then the meeting went on. As to whether Naser left, I was thinking about this. I think it seems to me that once we were told about the date, himself and Zulfo -- and this is something that I tried to think about last night and I think that him and Zulfo went out and they were whispering to one another and apparently Osman said: "This is the date and this is the time." But probably they had agreed something beforehand. I mean, this is just an assumption, because I have no idea, because we did not agree on the time, because Osman, as the chief, told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of my question, Mr. Meholjic, the essence of my question is the following: What Naser promised you when he said "you will get the time you need," this is something that others did not adhere to. Osman for example, can you agree?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can agree. I mean, at that meeting we got the information about the date. That's what I saw. I mean, I kept thinking about this last night. I think the attack took place on Monday and the meeting took place on Saturday. So it was two days later and I keep thinking about it and it keeps cropping up in my mind. So to me, this one day, basically not even two days, meant nothing and so I couldn't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to, once again, take a look at page 15046, below the title "the minutes of the meeting on the 3rd of October, 1992". Below that, item 1, it says "agreement about action." Item 2, "consultations with the Presidency." And then, "present, unit commanders." A short while ago we saw a name on page 3, the name Hamdija. It was Hamdija Fezic, wasn't it, the member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that when it came to consultations about actions, the War Presidency had considerable influence over all of that, am I right? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't insinuate that. I don't know. I've never been present at any consultations or talks within the Presidency. I can only think that they had influence, but I was never present there, because I was not allowed. I mean, Naser knows it. I mean, I didn't have such free access to certain things and I'm unable to say. I mean, I can't insinuate anything whatsoever. Especially if it's not true. It wouldn't be logical for the Presidency not to know about these things. There's no logic behind that. Because if you are planning to undertake a broad action, and especially if we're talking about this action in particular, and Mr. Oric is present here so he can speak for himself. But not everything is in the minutes. And I even don't know if these -- this is a faithful reproduction of the discussions, but even if it is, they did not take down every single word, because on the basis of this, you may think that this was a two-minute meeting, but there were preparations to go to look for food. And somebody, I think Suljo, had the task to get horses and go and look for food because people were starving and Suljo was a member of the Presidency and at the same time Suljo -- I can't remember his name. Hamed or something. He was secretary at the Defence secretariat. And his task, it seems to me, was to get the people to give him horses so that they could go and get some maize so that they had something to eat. But the Presidency was supposed to know. But perhaps they didn't know. I can't really claim anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you agree that Mr. Hamdija, as a member of the War Presidency, was present at that meeting and he was involved in the discussions there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree he was the president of the executive committee. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we did not have any chiefs or anything like that. We had the mayor and he was Hajrudin Avdic, and the president of the executive committee, and today it is done by others. I mean, they were in charge of the budget. At the time we had no budget at all. But the president of the executive committee was in charge of all that. He would have had to deal with the budget in much the same way as, just for the sake of a comparison, we have another -- treasurers, or whatever, today dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we set aside for a moment the influence that Naser Oric would have had to have as commander, keeping in mind his actual influence, could you agree that his influence on the occasion of these meetings, the meetings that you yourself attended, was not greater than Zulfo's, for example?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would just like to point out. I'm going to answer your question, you know. But no, it wasn't -- when I said it wasn't, this is why I said in the beginning that Naser Oric was not the person who was the appropriate choice of commander, because there were problems with people. You had to get them under control. I had no -- there was nothing personal I had against him. But I felt it was a bad idea to put a person in that position and he was not up to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just clarify it. You answered to my question his influence wasn't bigger. And we don't have the term bigger or greater in the transcript. I would just like you to clarify whether you actually did say --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Zulfo was a member of the Territorial Defence Staff, what they were discussing about it in there, I don't know. But Zulfo had an authority and he was just as free as I was to say I won't go along with this. And as to whether he said anything or not at that particular time at that particular meeting he did not. As to how they settled things amongst themselves, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings that you attended, could you notice that his influence was not greater than the influence of Akif Ustic, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo's influence was greater than Akif's and Akif's was slightly less significant. But Akif could also say, "No." Because that's the way he was. But he was a member of that Staff and I really don't know how they settled things amongst themselves. They probably had difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not correct that the best you can say about these meetings is that different people, different commanders discussed matters pertaining to actions amongst themselves and that they were more or less in a position to convince others that their point of view was the correct one. Is that correct, on the basis of your experience of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not all that clear to me. Could you clarify it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat it. At those meetings, commanders discussed and coordinated things amongst themselves and each and every one of them was trying to impose his own opinion. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they had to impose their views, because they had better knowledge of their own areas. They knew what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Meholjic, it was not a matter of Staff meetings -- and I'm referring to the meetings that you yourself were attending -- whereby Naser as commander would simply say, "Okay, you are to do this. You are to do that." And they would obey his orders?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know how they organised things within the Staff. But when there were extended meetings, if there were extended meetings and so we are invited as well, not just members of the Staff proper, but extended meetings, as I said, well, in that case it would be the way you said. And when they were amongst themselves, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked about meetings that you yourself attended.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
