utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, I'm going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before we move to another topic, because the answer -- yes, on its own leaves the question unanswered, according to me. Could we go through it again, Madam Vidovic, please. Your question was this: So Mr. Meholjic, it was not a matter of Staff meetings - and I'm referring to the meetings that you yourself were attending - whereby Naser as commander would simply say, okay, you are to do this. You are to do that. And they would obey his orders. First, he said "no" and then he said "yes". So when you pointed out that you were referring specifically and exclusively to the meetings that he attended, he said "yes". But I don't know what he's saying "yes" to. Perhaps you can answer the question now, Mr. Meholjic. If I haven't made myself clear, please, I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I understood it was that Madam here asked whether it was true that, when I attended meetings, Naser did not stand up and order people to do this, that and the other. And I said "yes." Her question was whether it was true. And I said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clarify, Your Honour. My question is not translated properly, because I asked whether Naser was ordering, in the same way, actually, as the witness has just repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it seems to be clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has answered the question at this point. I don't think I need any clarification, further clarifications. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I am not quite clear yet. I would like to have a clarification. Am I correct in assuming that you would only talk about meetings which you attended, that at that meetings, there have been discussions between you and other commanders and where Naser would say something, or would not say something? But you did not deal with meetings in other groups, where you have not been present. So you did not make, make a statement with regard to Staff meetings that you have not been present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say anything about things that I did not attend. I think it would be logical for the Staff to sit down to consider requests, demand by the War Presidency to search for food because the people were starving and that they would take a decision saying, we took a decision to attack this position and then this is the presumption that they would have, that nobody can convene me to nothing. My presumption is that they would have prepared something in advance, some decision, et cetera. So we did not propose. I believe that proposals were drafted beforehand. I did not attend that meeting, but I did attend the meeting where the agreement was reached. Whether there were any previous meetings, I cannot tell you about them because I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I will now switch on to another topic. You were asked a series of questions on the establishment of the War Presidency of Srebrenica. I would like to ask the usher to show the witness Prosecution evidence P42. Could you take a look at this document. This is a document, a decision, alleged decision of the War Presidency, dated 1st of July, 1992. You -- in your testimony you said that you did not attend that meeting when the War Presidency was established, and also that people did not tell you many things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when the War Presidency was established, but the latter part of the question, when people would not tell me many things, could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you said -- or let me rephrase it. Would you agree that some people in Srebrenica, up to a certain extent for this or other reasons that you don't have to explain now, maybe kept you in the dark? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sometimes. On many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The evidence doesn't make sense, unless it is explained. What people in Srebrenica? To what extent? For what reasons? And about what topics was he kept in the dark? Otherwise it's incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we are not going to comment on that, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be incomprehensible to you. We are not saying whether it is incomprehensible to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received many information from Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not arrive to Srebrenica before August 1992, so that maybe you did not have correct information on the establishment of the War Presidency. Can you accept that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have. Maybe later on I had some post facto information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you did testify on certain information that you had pertaining to this event and, in this light, I will ask you the following question, please. It is known to you, is it not, that at that meeting, at the beginning of July 1992, leading persons of the SDA of Srebrenica took part, like Hamdija Fezic, Hajrudin Avdic. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did take part. I don't know were they -- whether were they among the leaders of SDA. What I consider leadership are two, three people. But at that time they did not lead the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But they were among the leaders of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look at this decision. Please take a look at the preamble, the introductory part. The first sentence, it is stated there: Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to declare a state of war, and after that, at the initiative of the armed forces and citizens of the free territory of Srebrenica. In connection with this I will ask you the following question. Regarding the establishment of the War Presidency, you were the person who, in fact, suggested that civilian authority were established, including War Presidency. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it went for an initiative inter alia of citizens, including you, yourself, because you were not a member of the Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica. Is it not --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a part of the establishment. I proposed this. I was not a member of the staff of the Territorial Defence, but I did suggest that it should be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, maybe you misunderstood me. I was speaking about the initiative.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So as a citizen you endorsed this initiative?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, when the War Presidency was established, military police was established as well. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't known before I saw some documents, but it was around at the same time. I do not contest that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the military police, from its inception, was part of the public security station, that Mirzet was subordinated to Mr. Halilovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not correct. It was not proper for a chief of civil police to be chief of military police. He shouldn't have accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But de facto this was so, in practice?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are very important things for me. Subordinated to Mr. Bogilovic. And it was translated "Halilovic.". So it is fifth line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I noticed that immediately, Madam Vidovic. I went straight on to the monitor. So it shouldn't be "Halilovic" it should be "Bogilovic." Correct? Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is enough. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I will show you a document. Please, Madam Usher, would you be so kind to show the witness a document. It is a document drafted by the republic of Srpska. Public security station of Srebrenica. Dated 22nd of October 1996. RR146579. It goes for an official note. Please produce it. There is a description of a number of documents there, found by Serbian authorities after the fall of Srebrenica. I would like to ask you a question pertaining to a small section of that document. Please take a look at page 2 of that document, Mr. Meholjic. Page 2. In the penultimate passage on page 2, it says -- an I will quote, please take a look at the penultimate passage, it says here: On a piece of paper commander of the SJB, Jusuf Nurija, asked from Avdic to give him advice how to go about with non-persons of Serb ethnicity who are detained by him and who originate from Karna. I will not ask you questions about this piece of paper, but I will, however, ask you this: Mr. Jusuf Nurija was commander of the -- he was subordinated to Becir Bogilovic and he was head of the SJB. These events --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These events took place in early summer 1992, the events surrounding the village of Karna; is it true?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document to your knowledge -- have you heard that some persons were detained at the public security station in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you. At that time, I was not allowed to gain access to the police station, because I was considered an enemy. And about these things, I have no knowledge. And I responsibly can say, in front of this Trial Chamber, that no paperwork was found by me when I came on the 26th of April, 1993 when I was appointed chief. I don't know whether these documents are true. Maybe this was true. Maybe not. I'm not doubting. But what I'm saying is that within the police station, I did not take over any paperwork from Mr. Bogilovic when I assumed my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a series of questions pertaining to what you just said. But I'm simply asking you this, there were actions taking place around Karna; is it true?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tender this document, assign it an exhibit number as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being admitted in evidence and is being marked as Defence Exhibit D245.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the usher to show the witness an excerpt from P84, war diary. Page 5075. 5075.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is -- it starts on page 24 in the -- no. Sorry. It starts on page 24 in the English version, and finishes on page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the English version, I believe that's page 25. Please take a look. It's an excerpt from minutes of the meeting of the Staff of Armed Forces, dated 10th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you see this date?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, you don't have to pay attention to that date. I'm just telling you that this is an excerpt from minutes of the meeting from 10th of November, but I will ask you something else concerning this. Please take a look. On this page, under Roman II, cooperation with the military police is good. Then you -- as another line marker, the name Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there is a smudge here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out to you. Zulfo says: "Good policemen are not necessary to certain individuals," but in connection with the next quote I will ask you the question. So please pay attention to this quote. "Who let Ahmo's people to go to the prison is no longer in the police." Carry out an investigation into this young had from Bajramovici. Mirza says that he carried out the preliminary procedure and the record was delivered to Becir. Therefore, Mirza is Mirzet Halilovic, is he not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are no other Mirzas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this I will ask you this question. It is true, isn't it, that the person that conducted the preliminary procedure - in our Criminal Procedure Act, is another term for police investigation - that such a person would always submit their report to their superior officer?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is supposed to be so [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meholjic, it was entered into the transcript "Yes. This is supposed to be so."

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he must know as a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the question -- I would like the transcript to be corrected to this effect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were appointed as chief of the public security service, you found military police within the structures of the civil police?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day. And then I threw them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had problems in getting rid of military police when you were appointed the chief of public security.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had complications but I threw them out. They would not enter my building. If I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some problems. Atif Krdzic, when Mirza got killed, I had some problems but I said: "Get out from here."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Meholjic, in fact military police had before your appointment -- part of civil police; am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the way it is reported in the transcript, but anyway, I think it -- we can understand what is -- pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would it be "were part."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can't help it, Mr. Di Fazio. I mean I can't - otherwise I would have to stop every minute with regard to the transcript. So let's move. We know exactly what the witness said. Yes, Madam Vidovic? That's the problem that arises when you don't allow this blessed interval of time between question an answer. This is the problem. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, you clearly stated that before your appointment, military police was part of civil police, within the ranks of civil police?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is not a contentious matter. I repeated that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. When you were appointed and when you assumed your position of chief of public security station, you did not find any records, any documents, statements, depositions, any cases formulated. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I notified Ministry of the Interior through the package device. I did not find anything. There were no criminal charges against persons unknown or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Simply documentation had not been completed, records had not been kept before demilitarisation, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well if Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's not a question, unless this witness can tell us how he knows that they weren't kept, then I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All he know is: I came along. I don't see anything. He doesn't know if they were kept or taken away or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're perfectly right, perfectly right, Mr. Di Fazio. Yes, Madam Vidovic. One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put it to you this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, provided that there were minutes on the interrogation of prisoners of war, minutes of -- interviews of certain witnesses, any criminal charges, had they been there you would have been in a position to see them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I did not find anything there. Who I found was commander of the police station who had been appointed in December. He was there in the pre-war period. Mr. Mustafic, and I asked him, "Did you keep any records?" And he said "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find them. I don't know whether they'd been kept, but I did not find them. I did not receive anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The said Mustafic told you that no records had been kept?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was commander of civil police before the war and, in 1992, in December, he was reinstated as commander of civil police. And Becir was his superior officer. And since he was there during my term of office, I asked him and he said "no," and I was surprised that there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a professional policeman, you must have performed the transfer of duty with your predecessor, Mr. Becir Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Becir just left. There was no official transfer. And there was nothing to transfer. Every -- case files were dishevelled all over the place and I had to sort it all out. Nothing was transferred to me. I prepared a record of that and forwarded it to the Ministry of the Interior Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Tuzla and then they forwarded it to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said "files" we are talking about pre-war files, records of citizens, is it not so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to other countries within -- in our country, police stations issued ID cards, driver's licenses, permits to carry weapons, permits to transport explosives, because there were mines in the area. So all kinds of permits were issued by the police. So this is why we had files on IDs, driver's licenses, passports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me, won't you that armed -- or military forces, after the agreement on demilitarisation had to leave the city of Srebrenica, the core of the area of Srebrenica, is it not --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you correctly. We had to disarm, but we had nothing -- nowhere to withdraw to. It was like a bucket. We had no place to retreat to. We had to disarm on the 18th of April, 1993. Ramiz conducted negotiations as far as I know with UNPROFOR and he congregated us to inform us how we were to go about disarming. After that I went to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good. Military police was disbanded and it was decided that civil police should take over its duties, so the remnants of military police was disbanded after the demilitarisation; am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask the usher to show the witness a document. It is an assessment of the political security situation in the Srebrenica enclave, dated 23rd of May, 1995 prepared by the public security station of Srebrenica. Mr. Meholjic, please take a look at this document. The first page, and then the second page, it says Hakija Meholjic." Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please go through the document.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer my question whether it is -- goes for a document that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will quote the second paragraph of this document. Not to lose too much time. "Both military and civilian police operated in Srebrenica during combat operations, but police work was reduced to detaining the perpetrators of misdemeanours and crimes for three days and then releasing them without filing reports, because no court, misdemeanour court, Prosecutor's office or prison existed at the time. After UNPROFOR came to the Srebrenica enclave and it was demilitarised, the military police ceased to operate and only civilian police was left in operation. Municipal republic Prosecutor's office, lower court, miss demeanour court and prison were established, as well as other government authorities. When military police ceased to operate, it was a agreed with the 8th OG command that civilian police would maintain law and order, prevent crime, detect perpetrators of misdemeanours and criminal offences, and file reports against both civilian and military perpetrators with the misdemeanour court and the Srebrenica municipal public Prosecutor's office. And the courts in Srebrenica would process urgent investigations and maintain contact with the military court in Tuzla. Therefore military police, after the fall of Srebrenica, was not authorised to conduct any sort of investigation. Is it so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica itself, not any person could do so who was a member of the military, including military security?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- the question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Members of military security service, if any, could not have operated in Srebrenica because of the demilitarisation; is it so?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not operate to perform their duties publicly, let's be frank here. They could not do so openly, to operate openly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like this assessment of the political security situation in the Srebrenica enclave to be designed [as interpreted] an exhibit number, and to be tendered into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and that will be Defence Exhibit D246. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the usher, while she is still on her feet, to show the witness the document 018460655. It is an act of the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality, dated 28th of February, 1994, signed by Salihovic, Fahrudin. Let me correct this number. Computer number 01840655. Mr. Meholjic, please take a look at this document. I will quote. It is a very short document. I will quote it for you. It was adopted on the 28th of February, 1994 and it says, "The Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica at its session on 28th of February, 1994, adopted the following decision. The work reports for 1993 of the following are hereby adopted. First, the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica municipality - command of the 8th OG Srebrenica number 50/94, of the 2nd of February, 1994, and under 2, the municipal prison in Srebrenica, number 1/94 of the 10th of January, 199" -- presumably 94 because the last digit is illegible. Please, Mr. Meholjic, this document confirms, does it not that the prison provided separate reports to the War Presidency and the staff of the armed forces a separate report to the War Presidency for their work in 1993. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but this pertains for the period from the establishment of the prison, which was under the justice ministry as an outpost of the Tuzla prison. But we reported that because the Presidency had to take decisions on how to feed them, et cetera. This was an inception report to explain to them what -- how many people were there. But since this was a political structure, we had to prepare reports to their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like this document to be tendered into evidence and be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this document will become Defence Exhibit D247.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on and ask you the following. It is true, isn't it, Mr. Meholjic, that the War Presidency tried to establish something that should have been a military court. They called it a court martial. They did make certain attempts to that effect?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me about that. I only heard that this had been established. I was not a member of the Presidency. This happened at the beginning of 1992. I learned that from Djemo Becirovic. We spoke and he told me that this had been established. I don't know whether there had been any trials conducted by that court. I only heard that I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, your answer is actually the essence of my question. This court or an institution of that kind never became operational.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I heard "court martial" I thought that I would be tried by that court, by the -- that I would be condemned to death by them, because court March hall is something that you feared. Court martial is something intimidating and that's why I was interested to see what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question, Mr. Meholjic, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being put to you that this court martial or this court or this institution - that's how Madam Vidovic referred to it now - in actual fact never saw the light of day. It never became operational. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have answered that I don't know of anybody ever having been tried by that court. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did say "no," but this has not entered the transcript, but subsequently he has clarified. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness another document which is Prosecutor's Exhibit P162.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is information by the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality, the date is 25th, May, 1993 and this was sent to the Presidency of the Tuzla district. Mr. Meholjic, please take a look at this document. I am going to quote just one paragraph, from this document. It is a long document. We would like not to waste any more time than we need. I am going to quote page 0618, paragraph 3 from the bottom of that page. Please look at the third paragraph from the bottom of that page. And I am going to ask you whether you will agree with some of the facts that are stated herein. I'm quoting: "You are familiar of the situation that we were in in Srebrenica in the past time. We did not receive any official visit or any regulations, so the decrees that you're referring are unknown to us, official gazettes number 1 or 2/93 that you sent to us are the first sets of regulations that we received from the very beginning of the war." And later on, can you please look at the last paragraph in which it says as follows, on the same page that, is: "We are addressing you with a request to for your assistance in organising the judicial powers in Srebrenica. In Srebrenica we have no judges or prosecutors left. The public security station in Srebrenica is staffed to perform duties pertaining to its purview to carry out pre-trial procedures and to file criminal reports." And then, can you please turn the document to the next page and look at the first two short paragraphs. I am going to quote. It says: "Since we don't have Prosecutors or regular general courts or military courts, we are asking you to contact the republic secretariat for justice and administration and provide us with instructions on how to proceed. We would like to remind you that so far we've had many serious crimes. The administration organs are not sufficiently staffed as well. Please forward to us all the necessary regulations, especially those adopted in 1992 and 1993." In connection with this, let me ask you the following, Mr. Meholjic. Do you agree with me, if I say that the Prosecution bodies and courts could not function without any regulations or laws?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, there were none to be had, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were none. And I already said that this was established when I came. Before that there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The quote that you've just heard from me and that I quoted, the information of the War Presidency, testifies to the fact that the public security station in Srebrenica that you were the head of was staffed only to file criminal reports. Will you agree with me if I say that you, yourself, in the performance of your pre-trial procedures encountered huge difficulties?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I had difficulties. We were not equipped. We did have staff, but we did not have any equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with another document. The number of this document is 01838107. This is an enactment issued by the public security station of Srebrenica. It's number is 56/94. The date is 2 July 1994. This is a report on the work of the public security station of Srebrenica for the period starting with the 18th of April 1993 and through 31st December 1993. It was sent to the ministry of the interior inside Sarajevo, to the centre of security services in Tuzla, and the presidents of the municipality. First of all, Mr. Meholjic, please look at this report and to see whether this was -- this is your signature, and to see whether this is a report that you yourself drafted and signed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a long report. It would take me time to look at it properly. But this should be my signature. Yes, this is my document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Thank you, Mr. Meholjic. I'm going to read --

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell by the sentences that this is my style of expression. And that's why I've said that -- I'm not so sure about the signature, but I believe that it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read out to you one part of this document, part from page 1. It says in here, "in performing our regular tasks and the duties pertaining to our purview, based on laws and regulations enforced in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina until the war, this service had difficulties in terms of implementation of these regulations. It had to operate and adjust to the war conditions and was unable to implement all the current regulations. These problems were reflected in the disfunctioning of other supporting services, organs, and institutions, including communications equipment, inadequate equipment and insufficient number of good quality, i.e. professional policemen. Destruction of areas, documentation and a lack of basic tools for work. And also the disfunctioning of the lower and municipal courts and various technical services that were a prerequisite for the appropriate pre-war peacetime operation of the station. "In addition to all of the above deficiencies, the Srebrenica police station workers carried out duties which were not the responsibility of this service, such as: Providing security for Serbian families, the premises of the Red Cross," and so on and so forth. Before I put the question to you in connection with this, yesterday you mentioned the fact that security was provided for Serbian families which had been agreed with Oric. And this document confirms that, does it not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me ask you the following. It has to do with this subject matter. Do you agree with me that the situation was exactly as you described it in this document of yours?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I did and whatever I still do, I adhere to all that and I agree that the situation was exactly as described herein.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no teams for investigation, there was no equipment for criminal investigation of clues, there were no experts and so on an so forth?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no experts with -- we could not have that. Sometimes it was very difficult to go to the separation lines in order to carry out investigation. That was very difficult. Secondly, we could not leave the protected area. You could not send your policemen to get killed outside the protected area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true, therefore, that the other services were also not functioning, the ones that were -- that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't function and this aggravated our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't have paper, you didn't have any machinery, you didn't have computers?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In drafting this report, I was helped by the international police. They provided me with paper and also UNPROFOR provided me with paper in order for me to be able to draft my reports, because I used this paper to draft my criminal reports on it. I couldn't do it by hand. They were the only ones who helped me in any way, the only assistance I got was from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation. I would like to tender this document into evidence. It was issued by the public security station in Srebrenica. I would like the document to be given the -- an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I clarify something here? Here it says that we are supposed to provide security for the Serbian families. They were citizens, but this was not possible to be done. However, we believed that these people should be protected because there were people from other areas, a lot people from other areas that could cause problems and that's why these people were guarded around the clock. And this was another thing that made our job even more difficult. Naser and I agreed -- and I remember that we visited a person in Orasanin [phoen]. We talked to him and we told him that if he noticed anything, that he should report to us. This person, his name is Stanisa and he can confirm that. He is still alive and living in Srebrenica. He can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document will become Defence Exhibit D 248.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Meholjic, that the -- any sort of investigation under this condition was close to impossible?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it was difficult, but we did what we could. It is up to somebody else to be a judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was easier for you to come by information if people were willing to provide you with information, wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it would. The information was provided in the most primitive way. The most primitive way was to obtain information directly. There were no ballistic experts [as interpreted] that could provide us with information. Only in our work with people and through the goodwill of those people we were able to obtain information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meholjic, do you agree with me that during that period of time, in Srebrenica, throughout all this time as a matter of fact, throughout the war, there was fear amongst Muslims and hatred towards the Serbs that had prosecuted [as interpreted] them and it was very difficult to obtain any information on a crime that was committed against the Serbs? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. There were very few sensible people. Those who would appreciate that, not all people were the same and there are good and bad people on all sides, irrespective of their ethnic background. I told you when -- yesterday when we were talking about Halilovic, the man who committed three murders, when I detained him I had a I had problems, who committed three murders, when I detained him -- a I had problems, I was attacked by his family from Potocari so that I even had to ask for UNPROFOR protection. I believe that UNPROFOR has records of -- to that effect, because they obviously had to record everything that happened on the ground. They had to maintain records as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the transcript is not clear on a very important matter. I said to you amongst Muslims there was fear and hatred against the Serbs who had persecuted them. And it was very difficult -- again, I am using the word "Serbs who had expelled them from their areas," if the interpreter can understand me. "Serbs who had expelled them from their areas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was clear enough from the very beginning, because it doesn't make sense to see "prosecuted" there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, do you agree with me when I say that the information on crimes was much easier to obtain if such a crime was committed against the Muslims and their property? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us something about refugees, about tens of thousands of refugees in a very small area of Srebrenica. It is correct, is it not, that these people had arrived from different -- mixed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came from everywhere and their mentalities differed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You people from Srebrenica did not know them, did you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know them. I was a foreigner in my own town, because there was more of them than of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very often they didn't know each other, did they?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They came from different municipalities some of which were a hundred kilometres away, so they didn't know each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No official records were kept on those refugees as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was done at the request of the UNHCR that a list was compiled, but if had been done, this was done by the civilian protection. But this happened only later on, towards the end of 1994 or beginning of 1994. I can't be sure of that. There were -- there was some documentation. We were talking about 45.000 people who were registered as refugees in that enclave. 8.000 had been transferred by UNPROFOR when Srebrenica was demilitarised and when the Serbian forces allowed some of the population to exit the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, let's just clarify one thing. Until the year 1994, there was no such official record on the refugees as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no official records.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The refugees did not have addresses. They slept where they could. They stayed where they could. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. For some of the people we knew their addresses. The others slept where they could. There was 16 people sleeping in one room at places. And this is nothing new. This is something that has been recorded by a number of journalists who came to visit us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Meholjic, that under such conditions it was very difficult to obtain information on what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning. Later on, we had somewhat better coordination when the zone became demilitarised. At the beginning there was a lot of misinformation. It was very difficult to know what was going on on the ground. Of course, this is only normal. Under such conditions we're talking about a very huge area, too big for us to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said at the beginning, you are referring to the period before the demilitarisation. You are saying that that period was particularly chaotic? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meholjic, yesterday you told us that you had filed a criminal report against Amir Halilovic and that UNPROFOR had transferred him to Tuzla. You also told us that you had filed a criminal report for the murders committed at the beginning of 1993, at the time when you were not the chief, but you had obtained that information. You also told us that Oric assisted you with that. In this connection, I would like to ask you as follows: It is true, is it not, Mr. Meholjic, that you would have filed criminal reports for the crimes, including war crimes, providing that you had any sort of reliable information and evidence to the effect that these crimes had been committed irrespective of the fact who had committed them. Am I right in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saying that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. But somebody would have had to inform -- inform me about that. I would have had to obtain information in order to -- in order for the investigation to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you had reliable evidence that Amir Halilovic had committed these crimes and you filed a criminal report? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no reason for you not to do that, even in other cases, if you had any issue about the crimes having been committed. I'm talking about you personally?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are referring to the citizens and soldiers of Serbian origin. I believe that you are referring to them. In Srebrenica there should be a criminal report that I issued against a Muslim, Begovic, who was Huso's son. He cursed a Serbian. He cursed his mother. He was reported and imprisoned. And in a daily there is a report on me being an enemy of the Muslims for having reported this guy and for this guy having ended in prison. This should exist. There are records on all the reports that I filed and really, it didn't matter which ethnic group they belonged to. I told you already that whatever I learnt, I issued and ordered -- an order for the things to be processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. That was the essential of my question. Your Honours, I believe that this is a good moment for our next Your Honours I believe that this is a good moment for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, I think the witness can be escorted, unless you want to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to, but the witness can be taken out. It doesn't concern him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just this. I don't know if Madam Vidovic is going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But whatever the situation, whether she does or does not, I -- first I reiterate more strongly than ever that I would like to -- if she does finish early, that I would like to start my re-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your wish will be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If she does not finish, then I would like to be able to address you about re-examination perhaps at about 1.40 or thereabouts. So could we finish, if she's still -- if Madam Vidovic is still with the witness, could we ask the witness to leave because there is something I want to raise with you about the nature of re-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. We will have a break of 25 minutes. Usher. The usher has -- registrar, officer, could you give the registrar, please, the mobile that was -- you have in your pocket which was ringing at ten minutes to 12. You will get it back from your chief later on. Can you check for me whether it is switched on or off.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can't even open it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see. Leave it as it is and please hand it to Mr. Innell soon after the sitting. Thank you. 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, in the course of your testimony you described and you confirmed it upon seeing the document, that after demilitarisation the regular Tribunal was set up at Srebrenica as well as the Prosecution office, the Prosecutor's office, but you will agree with me that that court was -- did not have competence to deal with serious crime, including looting, murder and similar crime?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Especially, they did not have competences to deal with crimes

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Especially, they did not have competence to deal with crimes which would fall within the competence of a military court?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because you can see in the report that they -- the Prosecutor held talks with the military court at Tuzla and they dealt with it. I had no competence in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Clear. Thank you. However, since that court was not even able to deal with their own cases for the simple reason that they did not enjoy the necessary conditions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, if what you have in mind are the conditions with regard to the penal or criminal law that we have inherited from before, because there were no major changes. But there were financial penalties, for example, provided for, but you could not impose financial penalties since nobody had any money. So it was simply impossible to pass certain sentences. But the judges did what they could. In case it was an infringement or a crime which was a bit more serious, they sent people to prison for a couple of days, that was against the law as well. And so that is based on what I know. And then we submitted reports against citizens of Bosnian nationality and there was no other solution there. It is better to do something rather than nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the exhibit, the Defence Exhibit D243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Vidovic, how much more time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've made good progress, but this precisely is the part where we need to deal with several documents. If I don't finish up today, I will certainly need very little time on Monday, no longer than 20 minutes, unless I manage to finish up today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes. Has the witness been given the document, D243? Yes. This is one of the documents we -- that were tendered this morning? No? The first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to quote to you the second and the third paragraph on the page, which ends at 9097 and I'm quoting. "To expect better situation and better conditions, we cannot expect a better situation or facilitate the operation of civilian authorities unless we are physically connected to Tuzla. The absence of a second-instance court means that unsolved cases keep piling up at the court, which negatively affects the atmosphere, because citizens believe they will not be held accountable, so decide to get involved in all sorts of criminal activities. The absence of military police and a military court is a great problem and army members resent being reported by civilian police, which puts the Srebrenica public security station into an awkward position. Lacking minimum living conditions in the enclave, in their struggle for survival, people destroy factories, rip off roofs, doors, et cetera, to build their own living quarters. Although civilian authorities have been doing everything to improve the situation and to protect factories, they have not had much success. People have also been usurping state properly destroying forests and especially evergreen forests. Such phenomena, we're trying to stop these phenomena by submitting criminal reports, but the lack of functioning and the absence of a second-instance court makes it more difficult." Mr. Meholjic, before we move on to talk about this, I would just like to ask you the following: Does the text that I have read out to you in the last part of the text where there is a description of the behaviour of the citizens within Srebrenica itself, them ripping off roofs and doors, et cetera, does this actually reflect the real state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no problem. It does reflect the real, state of affairs, I did write it down and I still stand by it because I did not have enough police officers to place them in front of other -- each house and each factory. And I was not able to cover all of that. I mean, everything that is indicated in this document is proper account of the situation. I did not invent anything. I didn't write it haphazardly. There were discussions about whether we should send this in, because those were harsh words, but we nevertheless managed to send it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question is this, not even within Srebrenica itself, you could not really do anything about these people. You couldn't stop them destroying Muslim property. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just going to quote you one example. My father was hosting a refugee and there were cherries in the cherry tree, and the guy climbed up the tree and he broke off all the branches. And so nobody else could get to the cherries, and we had no electricity. We had no street lighting. There was nothing and there were too many people loitering about, day and night. So it was a huge problem and I mean later on I found out that even some Serb forces were coming in and they were mixing with the population to see what it was like. I mean I found out about that later because it was simply impossible to follow all of these developments. It was impossible to introduce a curfew or anything. So the situation was really extremely difficult. There was a total lack of discipline on the part of the citizens and especially on the part of certain individuals and certain commanders. So all of that had an impact on the situation and the overall atmosphere and the fact that we're in a closed off area. I mean it is up to experts to say in what way it determines the peoples' state of mind. I can just, you know say that I stand by everything I've written in this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to what we had mentioned before. So basically, under such conditions, not a single trial could have been completed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our legal provisions, which we had inherited from the former Yugoslavia since there was nothing else, those who were sentenced in the first instance had to write to appeal to the court of second instance and so we did not have a court of second instance. So a sentence might have been imposed, but then they would have wanted to appeal. But they would have had to go to Sarajevo to appeal. But we did not have a physical link there. So there was no court of second instance. So objectively speaking it was a very difficult situation for the judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that there was no physical link or connection to Tuzla. The links, the communications that you've mentioned were not sufficient in order to make for an even halfway sufficient flow of information with Tuzla. There was no possibility to send in any evidence to Tuzla in that way; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, maybe in some instances, maybe if we had separate situations for the police, for the Staff, of the municipality. Well, no it wasn't possible. There was no such possibility. This one Paket radio system could not deal with that. So we tried to do what we could as best we could, but always whilst trying to talk to the higher authorities at Tuzla, the judiciary, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well here I am talking simply about the period after I was appointed chief of police. Apart from that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your last point refers to the period of time starting in April 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked to us about the functioning of the communication systems. You said that in 1992 there was a radio station and somebody called Naser used to work there. Do you know, by any chance, if this was Naser Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He's bald. He has not hair at all. He's tiny, but I don't know him really. He is not from the area of Srebrenica. I mean, I know now who he is but I don't know his family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know his name is Naser.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you accept that since that radio device was used by you yourself only ones, at least that is my understanding of the situation, that you did not, in fact, have enough information about who supervised and was in charge of that radio station and in what way?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I talked to Djemo, I was told that that radio device was meant to cover the needs of the staff and the Presidency, and from my point of view that was only normal. There was nothing to argue about. Because if everybody were to come along there would have been a great deal of confusion and we needed some order. So that's the information I had, and I did not have any other information. Even though I did use it without asking anyone, because they told me they did manage to get in touch with my family and they were actually held somewhere else for eight months and I didn't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meholjic. Now I would like to ask the usher to show another document to the witness. The number is 01801624, and it is a document issued by the War Presidency of Srebrenica, number 85/92, dated the 1st of October, 1992. And the title is "the report." Mr. Meholjic, could you take a look at that document. At this particular moment we are not particularly concerned with the contents of the document. I would just like to ask you to look at the name of the author who drafted this, and it says there "Communications and Information Service of the Municipality of Srebrenica." Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this was not the communications service of the armed forces or the Staff of Srebrenica; can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't. I can tell you I don't know. You know why, I mean that's what it says on the paper and therefore it seems to be what you say. But I think that the staff would have had to use it. I don't know who was the sponsor, as it were. I don't know who was above them. But I do know, on the basis of my conversation with Djemo Becirevic, who was a member of the War Presidency, that this was meant to be used by the Presidency and the staff, and I know that Naser, at that time - I don't know at what time exactly - did talk to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Sefer Halilovic. As to whether he did or didn't, I don't know. That's what I heard from Djemo Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meholjic, I'm not trying to claim that staff did not make use of it. I'm simply drawing your attention, or rather, trying to ask you whether you were aware that there was a liaison or communication service at the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no board anywhere, plaque or anything stating that. I can't be very specific on that one, but it is logical, since it is indicated Presidency here, that it was the Presidency; if it was indeed because I've never seen this document before, I don't know, and I was far away from the real source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask somebody else who was a member of the Presidency or a member of the staff. They will probably know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we submit this into evidence, please, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document will become Defence Exhibit D249.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you mentioned that the radio Paket device was the property of the Territorial Defence staff and with respect to that I would like you to take a look at another document. I would like to ask the usher to show the witness the document coming from the War Presidency of Bratunac, of the 11th of July, 1994, addressed to the Assembly of BH, 01838914. Mr. Meholjic, this document is a full-page document and, at this moment, I'm not actually discussing the contents of the document. All I would like you to do would be to look at the very end of this document. On one of the pages it says: On behalf of the War Presidency of the municipality of Bratunac, the Mayor Alica Zajkun [phoen]. There is a stamp there and I would like you to look at the bottom-left corner can you see at the very end, on page 4, that is to say the last page where the signature is. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that in the bottom-left corner, it says "Paket approved by the president of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica, Fahrudin Salihovic."

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow, Mr. Meholjic, for the possibility that it may be right that the use of the Paket was approved by the War Presidency as well?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that was the case. I can't deny it. Probably. We used to call him -- no longer president, but chief or head, or mayor. It was a different term. And possibly he was in charge of that. He was Ramiz's brother, the one who dealt with the Paket device and Ahmetovic, Nedzad as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meholjic. I would like for this document to be submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document will become Defence Exhibit D250. 250. Madam Vidovic, please stop your questions at exactly five minutes past the half hour. In other words, at 1.35 so that we will deal with the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am switching to another topic. It would be very convenient for me to conclude my today's cross-examination, if it's possible, because I have one chapter in my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think there is no problem there. There is no problem there. You know that we try to accommodate you both as much as we can. Mr. Meholjic, we are going to stop here for today. We will continue on Monday. In the meantime relax, and Monday we will finish with you. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher, and during the weekend you will receive all the assistance you require to make your stay here in The Hague as relaxing as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There are two matters. Firstly the schedule for Monday. I can say this. I don't -- I think my re-examination is going to be more than a ten-minute fixing up, cosmetic aspects job. So I will be -- have a substantial re-examination, I think. That's the first point that I want to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important that we finish with this witness on Monday. The rest is relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And I -- of course, I am not going to do anything that will interfere with that, but I just want to flag that. It's not going to be five minutes' worth and I want to work in with Your Honours, I don't want to -- I want to make sure that I can adjust my re-examination to make sure that Your Honours are given -- well, sufficient time for any questions that you may have. So I would be grateful if you can provide me with my guidance on that. That's the first point. Second point is how far one can go in re-examination. I looked at the Rules. The Rules are silent other than simply boldly stating, well, you have examination, cross-examination, re-examination. And I know what the basic principle of re-examination is, to clarify matters in cross-examination. I don't need to -- there is no issue that's going to arise on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to change the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the Rules, the written Rules, the Rules that you and I and Mr. Jones are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All familiar with, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of course my re-examination will only deal with issues that arise, topics that arise, have arisen today and may arise on Monday. On the 23rd of March, during the course of re-examination of Mr. Bogilovic by Ms. Sellers, Your Honour had this to say at the point of interjection -- an objection I should say by Madam Vidovic. Your Honour said, "Now leading questions with permissible at this stage. They weren't permissible during examination-in-chief, but they are permissible now. Just like you, in cross-examination, can put leading questions." I can safely say that I can use that as a guide to my re-examination on Monday? And does -- and I would intend to possibly make reference to past statements of this witness. Now, if there is going to be a problem with that, then it would be better for me to know so that I can structure my re-examination accordingly over the weekend. That's the issue that I am raising.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Have you finished Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we would like to have an opportunity to look at the transcript again but I always understood the general principle to be that in re-examination, leading questions are not permitted any more than they are in examination-in-chief, because it's -- it's the party's own witness. I don't know if there is a mistake in the transcript, or if it was taken at that out of context. But that's clearly the principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was different. That was -- were you re re-examining at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes Your Honours, I was re re-examining Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, but we will come to this on Monday and we will give you a direction exactly as to what is, according to us, the proper pronouncement. And do I read you -- you do not intend to treat the witness as a hostile witness or anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not making that application, no. I don't think I can at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. This is because I want to make sure that I am understanding what you say, because you said that you wished to confront him with previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to -- well, I may need to do that if I carry out the re-examination in the manner in which I wish to do so. My point is this, the guiding principle that I will use is: I'm restricted to elucidating or getting further explanation of issues raised by Madam Vidovic in cross-examination. The means by which I do that is what I'm concerned about. Leading questions, the ability to use prior statements, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will deal with this on Monday morning. We will come back to you. The difference between the examination-in-chief and the re-examination is a very simple and straightforward one, that the re-examination and the right to re-examine the witness arises out of the questions put on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for -- just like cross-examination, arises out of the questions put during the examination-in-chief. Same principles do apply. But we will be more categorical Monday on this, and you will be -- you will know exactly how to proceed. But I'm putting you on notice that you will -- I will discuss it with Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt, obviously. But I don't think you will find us entertaining any idea to treat the witness as a hostile witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I will not be making that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making it clear, because it will be ... Is there anything else you would like to raise at this point? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe just to observe that, therefore, if prior statements are an issue there's going to have to be some basis for the Prosecution doing it. It's not something which follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making bot myself very clear, and I think both of you coming from common law jurisdictions, you know exactly what I mean. You have every right, at any stage, during the examination-in-chief, even to put to the witness prior statements. But again the purpose of doing that or the -- is limited, is limited by law. You can't do that to contradict or discredit the witness without following the usual procedure that I referred to earlier on, which has not been followed during the entire examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just if Your Honours want to look at that little page that I quoted to you, you will find it at page 6532 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So we adjourn till Monday morning at -- it is in the morning, isn't it? Yes, it is in the morning. Monday morning. I don't know which courtroom. Thank you. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of April, 2005 at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
